report:
## Does Regular Vitamin C Prevent Colds? — No, With Nuance

Your instinct is correct: for most people, regular vitamin C supplementation does **not prevent** colds. The strongest evidence comes from the **Cochrane systematic review** (Hemilä & Chalker, updated through 2013), which pooled 29 trial comparisons involving over 11,000 participants. It found that regular vitamin C intake had **no effect on cold incidence** in the general population (risk ratio ~0.97, essentially null) (cochrane.org, pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8078152/). Earlier pooled analyses of the six largest trials using ≥1 g/day similarly found no protective effect (pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9059230/).

There is one notable exception: people under brief, extreme physical stress—marathon runners, skiers, and soldiers in subarctic conditions—showed roughly a **50% reduction in cold incidence** with vitamin C. This effect doesn't hold for everyday populations, and researchers suggest it may relate to different causes of respiratory symptoms in extreme exertion (airway stress) rather than typical viral colds (nutraingredients.com; cochrane.org).

While vitamin C doesn't prevent colds for ordinary people, it does have a modest secondary benefit: regular (not therapeutic/after-onset) supplementation **shortens cold duration by about 8-9%** and may reduce symptom severity somewhat, per Cochrane and newer meta-analyses (link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12889-023-17229-8; pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38082300/). Starting vitamin C only after symptoms begin shows no benefit at all.

**Bottom line:** The evidence supports "no" — vitamin C does not meaningfully reduce your risk of catching a cold, except possibly under extreme physical exertion. It may modestly shorten a cold's duration if taken regularly beforehand.

**Sources:** cochrane.org/evidence/CD000980_vitamin-c-preventing-and-treating-common-cold; pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8078152/; pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9059230/; ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK279544/
